General Theory of Processes - Part 1

I have been attending a reading course on stochastic analysis led by Professor Ioannis Karatzas, where the students take turns in presenting a topic of their choice. I recently presented on Choquet's theory of capacities and its applications to measure theory and in the general theory of processes. This blog post is based on this presentation. I have freely copied[1] from many sources, but my primary reference are the (unfortunately unpublished) lecture notes by Prof. Karatzas.

Introduction

Kolmogorov laid the modern axiomatic foundations of probability theory with the German monograph Grundbegriffe der Wahrscheinlichkeitsrechnung which appeared in Ergebnisse Der Mathematik in 1933. This was a period of intense discussions on the foundations of probability, and a majority of probabilists at the time considered measure theory not only a waste of time, but also an offense to "probabilistic intuition" (Meyer, 2009). But by 1950, with the work of Doob in particular, these discussions of foundations had been settled.

Continuous-time processes, on the other hand, were difficult to tame even with measure theory: if a particle is subject to random evolution, to show that its trajectory is continuous, or bounded, requires that all time values be considered, whereas classical measure theory can only handle a countable infinity of time values. Thus, not only does probability depend on measure theory, but it also requires more of measure theory than the rest of analysis (Meyer, 2009).

The missing pieces of the puzzle, which will be the highlight of this and the next blog post, are the debut, section and projection theorems. These theorems are also indispensable in many applications, for instance in dynamic programming and stochastic control (Karoui and Tan, 2013).

To get a taste of these theorems, let's recall a famous error made by Lebesgue in the paper Sur les fonctions représentables analytiquement published in 1905. Consider the measurable space (R2,B(R2))(\mathbb R^2, \mathcal{B}(\mathbb R^2))(R2,B(R2)) and the projection map π\piπ given by R2∋(x,y)↦π(x,y)=y∈R.\mathbb R^2 \ni (x,y) \mapsto \pi(x,y) = y \in \mathbb R.R2∋(x,y)↦π(x,y)=y∈R. It is easy to see that for any open set OOO in R2\mathbb R^2R2, the set π(O)\pi(O)π(O) is also open in R\mathbb RR: Recall that the standard topology on R2\mathbb R^2R2 is same as the product topology on R2.\mathbb R^2.R2. By the definition of the product topology on R2\mathbb R^2R2, an open set OOO in R2\mathbb R^2R2 is of the form O=⋃i∈I⋂j∈JiUij×VijO = \bigcup_{i \in I} \bigcap_{j \in J_i} U_{ij} \times V_{ij}O=⋃i∈I​⋂j∈Ji​​Uij​×Vij​ for open Uij,VijU_{ij}, V_{ij}Uij​,Vij​ in R\mathbb RR, III arbitrary and JiJ_iJi​ finite. A simple argument gives π(O)=⋃i∈I⋂j∈JiUij\pi(O) = \bigcup_{i \in I} \bigcap_{j \in J_i} U_{ij}π(O)=⋃i∈I​⋂j∈Ji​​Uij​ which is open in R.\mathbb R.R. In fact, more generally, projection from any product space (with product topology) is an open map. Now it seems reasonable to expect that for any Borel set B∈B(R2)B \in \mathcal{B}(\mathbb R^2)B∈B(R2) its projection is also a Borel set in B(R)\mathcal{B}(\mathbb R)B(R), and Lebesgue assumed this in his paper. But, in fact, this is FALSE! The error was spotted in around 1917 by Mikhail Suslin, who realised that the projection map need not be Borel, and this lead to his investigation of analytic sets and to begin the study of what is now known as descriptive set theory (Almost Sure blog).

The problem is projection doesn't commute with countable decreasing intersection. For example, consider the decreasing sequence of sets Sn=(0,1/n)×R.S_n = (0, 1/n) \times \mathbb R.Sn​=(0,1/n)×R. Then π(Sn)=R\pi(S_n) = \mathbb Rπ(Sn​)=R for all nnn, giving ⋂n∈Nπ(Sn)=R\bigcap_{n \in \mathbb N} \pi(S_n) = \mathbb R⋂n∈N​π(Sn​)=R, but ⋂n∈NSn=∅\bigcap_{n \in \mathbb N} S_n = \varnothing⋂n∈N​Sn​=∅, giving π(⋂n∈NSn)=∅.\pi \left( \bigcap_{n \in \mathbb N} S_n \right) = \varnothing.π(⋂n∈N​Sn​)=∅. The measurable projection theorem stated next will be one of the highlights of this post.

Measurable Projection Theorem: Let (Ω,F,P)(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})(Ω,F,P) be a complete probability space, let (K,B(K))(K, \mathcal{B}(K))(K,B(K)) be a locally compact separable metric space endowed with the collection of its Borel sets, and denote by π\piπ the projection of K×ΩK \times \OmegaK×Ω onto Ω.\Omega.Ω. Then, for every B∈B(K)⊗FB \in \mathcal{B}(K) \otimes \mathcal{F}B∈B(K)⊗F, the projection π(B)∈F.\pi(B) \in \mathcal{F}.π(B)∈F.

Why is proving such results difficult? As mentioned above it's because projection doesn't behave nicely with intersections. Nevertheless, let us try to see how one might try to prove the above theorem. A standard approach in measure theory is to construct a collection like

E={S⊆K×Ω : π(S)∈F}\begin{aligned} \mathscr{E} = \{S \subseteq K \times \Omega\,:\,\pi(S) \in \mathcal{F}\}\end{aligned}E={S⊆K×Ω:π(S)∈F}​
which contains the sets satisfying the desired property, and show that it is a σ\sigmaσ-algebra containing a simple collection, say A\mathscr{A}A, such that it easy to show that elements of A\mathscr{A}A satisfy the desired property and A\mathscr{A}A generates B(K)⊗F\mathcal{B}(K) \otimes \mathcal{F}B(K)⊗F, because then we will have B(K)⊗F⊆E.\mathcal{B}(K) \otimes \mathcal{F} \subseteq \mathscr{E}.B(K)⊗F⊆E. To this end, let
A={S⊆K×Ω : S=E×F for E∈B(K), F∈F}.\begin{aligned} \mathscr{A} = \{S \subseteq K \times \Omega\,:\, S = E \times F \text{ for } E \in \mathcal{B}(K),\, F \in \mathcal{F}\}.\end{aligned}A={S⊆K×Ω:S=E×F for E∈B(K),F∈F}.​
Then it is easy to see that A⊆E\mathscr{A} \subseteq \mathscr{E}A⊆E, A\mathscr{A}A generates B(K)⊗F\mathcal{B}(K) \otimes \mathcal{F}B(K)⊗F and that A\mathscr{A}A is an algebra. If we could show that E\mathscr{E}E is a monotone class, then we would be done on account of monotone class theorem. Increasing sequences are easily handled, in fact if {Sn}n∈N⊆K×Ω\{S_n\} _ {n \in \mathbb N} \subseteq K \times \Omega{Sn​}n∈N​⊆K×Ω is any sequence, then
π(⋃n=1∞Sn)=⋃n=1∞π(Sn).\begin{aligned} \pi\left(\bigcup_{n=1}^\infty S_n\right) = \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty \pi(S_n).\end{aligned}π(n=1⋃∞​Sn​)=n=1⋃∞​π(Sn​).​
But if S1⊇S2⊇⋯S_1 \supseteq S_2 \supseteq \cdotsS1​⊇S2​⊇⋯, then in general we cannot say
π(⋂n=1∞Sn)=⋂n=1∞π(Sn).\begin{aligned} \pi\left(\bigcap_{n=1}^\infty S_n\right) = \bigcap_{n=1}^\infty \pi(S_n).\end{aligned}π(n=1⋂∞​Sn​)=n=1⋂∞​π(Sn​).​
Enter Choquet's theory of capacities. It provides the language to prove results like these. We know that every Borel measure μ\muμ on Rd\mathbb R^dRd (in fact, any Polish space) has the interior regularity (also known as tightness) property
μ(B)=sup⁡K∈K(Rd)K⊆Bμ(K),∀ B∈B(Rd),\begin{aligned} \mu(B) = \sup_{\substack{K \in \mathscr{K}(\mathbb R^d) \\ K \subseteq B}} \mu(K), \quad \forall \; B \in \mathcal{B}(\mathbb R^d),\end{aligned}μ(B)=K∈K(Rd)K⊆B​sup​μ(K),∀B∈B(Rd),​
where K(Rd)\mathscr{K}(\mathbb R^d)K(Rd) is the collection of all compact sets in Rd.\mathbb R^d.Rd. The Choquet's theory of capacities generalizes this approximation-from-below property, and distills those properties of measure that allow for such approximation to hold in very general settings. As we will see, monotonicity and continuity from above and below properties are at play here, and notions corresponding to complements or differences will be absent.

The next few sections will be very abstract and it is easy to lose sight of our goal. Some people enjoy this mental gymnastics, but even if you find this dry, the reward at the end will be worth the initial struggle. We start with Choquet's theory of capacities. The highlight of this part will be Choquet's capacitability theorem. To prove this major result we will need to define a lot of new terminology and prove some major results like Sierpiński's theorem and Sion's theorem. Armed with Choquet's capacitability theorem we will prove Measurable Section theorem which in turn will form the backbone of various other results in measure theory. These results in measure theory will then help us prove results in general theory of processes, but we will discuss this part in the next blog post.

Pavings and Mosaics

Definition 1: Let EEE be a nonempty set. A collection E\mathcal EE of subsets of EEE is called a paving if it closed under finite unions and finite intersections. The pair (E,E)(E, \mathcal E)(E,E) is then called a paved space.

The concept of paving generalizes the concept of algebra. As an example, if EEE is a topological space, then the collection of closed subsets of EEE forms a paving. As another example, if EEE is a Hausdorff space, then (E,K(E))(E, \mathscr K(E))(E,K(E)) is a paved space, where as before K(E)\mathscr{K}(E)K(E) denotes the collection of all compact sets in E.E.E.

It is easy to check that an arbitrary intersection of pavings is also a paving, and that the collection P(E)\mathfrak{P}(E)P(E) of all subsets of EEE is a paving. Thus for any collection A\mathcal{A}A of subsets of EEE, we can define the notion of paving generated by A\mathcal{A}A as the smallest paving of subsets of EEE that contains A\mathcal{A}A by simply defining it to be the intersection of all pavings of EEE containing A.\mathcal{A}.A.

Definition 2: For two paved spaces (E,E)(E,\mathcal{E})(E,E) and (F,F)(F,\mathcal{F})(F,F), the product paving of E\mathcal{E}E and F\mathcal{F}F, denoted by E⊗pF\mathcal{E} \otimes_p \mathcal{F}E⊗p​F, is a paving on E×FE \times FE×F generated by all rectangles R={A×B : A∈E,B∈F}.\mathcal{R} = \{A \times B \,:\, A \in \mathcal{E}, B \in \mathcal{F}\}.R={A×B:A∈E,B∈F}.

Using the fact that (A1×B1)∩(A2×B2)=(A1∩A2)×(B1∩B2)(A_1 \times B_1) \cap (A_2 \times B_2) = (A_1 \cap A_2) \times (B_1 \cap B_2)(A1​×B1​)∩(A2​×B2​)=(A1​∩A2​)×(B1​∩B2​) we see that R\mathcal{R}R is stable under finite intersections. Therefore, any element of E⊗pF\mathcal{E} \otimes_p \mathcal{F}E⊗p​F is of the form ⋃i=1nAi×Bi\bigcup_{i=1}^n A_i \times B_i⋃i=1n​Ai​×Bi​, where Ai∈EA_i \in \mathcal{E}Ai​∈E and Bi∈FB_i \in \mathcal{F}Bi​∈F for all i=1,…,n.i=1,\ldots,n.i=1,…,n.

Definition 3: Let EEE be a nonempty set. A collection of subsets of EEE which is closed under countable unions and countable intersections is called a mosaic.

The concept of mosaic generalizes the concept of σ\sigmaσ-algebra. Just like paving, it is easy to define the notion of mosaic generated by a collection. They will always occur in the context of a paving E\mathcal{E}E on E.E.E. We denote by E^\widehat{\mathcal{E}}E the mosaic generated by E.\mathcal{E}.E. E ⊗^pF\mathcal{E}\ \widehat{\otimes}_p \mathcal{F}E ⊗​p​F will denote the mosaic generated by the product paving E⊗pF.\mathcal{E} \otimes_p \mathcal{F}.E⊗p​F.

Just like with monotone class arguments in measure theory, the paving E\mathcal EE will be a simple collection of subsets of EEE for which it is easy to prove a property P.P.P. From here we will show that the elements of the mosaic E^\widehat{\mathcal E}E also satisfy P.P.P. Often E^\widehat{\mathcal E}E will be a σ\sigmaσ-algebra.

Henceforth the notation E\mathcal{E}E will be used for a paving on E.E.E.

Properties of pavings and mosaics

Just like the results connecting algebra and σ\sigmaσ-algebra, we have results connecting pavings and mosaics.

Lemma 1: If A∈EA \in \mathcal{E}A∈E implies Ac=E∖A∈E^A^\mathsf{c} = E \setminus A \in \widehat{\mathcal{E}}Ac=E∖A∈E, then E^=σ(E).\widehat{\mathcal{E}} = \sigma(\mathcal{E}).E=σ(E).
Follows immediately from the monotone class theorem.

As an example, if EEE is a separable, locally compact metric space, and E=K(E)\mathcal{E} = \mathscr{K}(E)E=K(E) is the collection of compact subsets of EEE, then this property holds. In fact, EEE can be a second-countable locally compact Hausdorff space. Then it is σ\sigmaσ-compact and every compact subset is closed. This implies that the open set given by the complement of a compact set is a countable union of compact sets. Combine it with the fact that an open subset of a locally compact and σ\sigmaσ-compact is itself σ\sigmaσ-compact to get that if A∈EA \in \mathcal EA∈E, then Ac∈E^.A^\mathsf{c} \in \widehat{\mathcal E}.Ac∈E.

Lemma 2: The mosaic E^\widehat{\mathcal{E}}E is the smallest collection of subsets of EEE that contains E\mathcal{E}E and is closed under countable increasing unions and under countable decreasing intersections. In other words, if M(E)\mathcal M(\mathcal{E})M(E) denotes the monotone class generated by E\mathcal{E}E, then E^=M(E).\widehat{\mathcal{E}} = \mathcal M(\mathcal{E}).E=M(E).

Since a mosaic is a monotone class and since E⊆E^\mathcal{E} \subseteq \widehat{\mathcal{E}}E⊆E, we have M(E)⊆E^.\mathcal M(\mathcal{E}) \subseteq \widehat{\mathcal{E}}.M(E)⊆E. Then since R\mathcal{R}R is a paving, Bn=⋃i=1nAi∈RB_n = \bigcup_{i=1}^n A_i \in \mathcal{R}Bn​=⋃i=1n​Ai​∈R for all n∈N.{n \in \mathbb N}.n∈N. Similarly for countable intersections.

Compact pavings

Recall a standard result from topology: a topological space XXX is compact if and only if for every collection C\mathcal CC of closed subsets of XXX having the finite intersection property (i.e., every finite sub-collection of C\mathcal CC has nonempty intersection), the intersection ⋂C∈CC\bigcap_{C \in \mathcal C} C⋂C∈C​C is nonempty. For our use case, we consider countable sub-collections.

Definition 4: Consider an arbitrary collection A\mathcal AA of subsets of E.E.E. It is called a compact collection if every countable sub-collection of elements in A\mathcal AA having the finite intersection property has non-empty intersection. A paving E\mathcal{E}E is a compact paving, if every decreasing sequence of nonempty elements of E\mathcal{E}E has a nonempty intersection.

It is easy to verify that a compact paving is a compact collection. As an example, if EEE is a separable metric space, the collection, K(E)\mathscr{K}(E)K(E), of all compact subsets of EEE is a compact paving. This follows immediately from the finite intersection characterization of a compact topological space stated above.

We define

Eδ:={⋂n∈NAn : An∈E for all n∈N}\begin{aligned} \mathcal{E}_\delta := \left\{\bigcap_{n \in \mathbb N} A_n\,:\,A_n \in \mathcal{E} \text{ for all } n \in \mathbb N\right\}\end{aligned}Eδ​:={n∈N⋂​An​:An​∈E for all n∈N}​
and note that if E\mathcal{E}E is a compact paving then so is Eδ.\mathcal{E}_\delta.Eδ​. Indeed, Eδ\mathcal{E}_\deltaEδ​ is a paving because for A=⋂n∈NAnA = \bigcap_{n \in \mathbb N} A_nA=⋂n∈N​An​ and B=⋂m∈NBmB = \bigcap_{m \in \mathbb N} B_mB=⋂m∈N​Bm​ in Eδ\mathcal{E}_\deltaEδ​,
A∪B=⋂n∈N⋂m∈N(An∪Bm)∈EδA∩B=⋂n∈N⋂m∈N(An∩Bm)∈Eδ,\begin{aligned} A \cup B &= \bigcap_{n \in \mathbb N} \bigcap_{m \in \mathbb N} (A_n \cup B_m) \in \mathcal{E}_\delta \\ A \cap B &= \bigcap_{n \in \mathbb N} \bigcap_{m \in \mathbb N} (A_n \cap B_m) \in \mathcal{E}_\delta,\end{aligned}A∪BA∩B​=n∈N⋂​m∈N⋂​(An​∪Bm​)∈Eδ​=n∈N⋂​m∈N⋂​(An​∩Bm​)∈Eδ​,​
and Eδ\mathcal{E}_\deltaEδ​ is a compact paving because intersection of a sequence of countable intersections is again a countable intersection.

The next lemma tells us when it acceptable to commute projection with countable intersections.

Envelopes

Definition 5: Let (E,E)(E, \mathcal{E})(E,E) be a paved space, and fix a subset A⊆EA \subseteq EA⊆E as well as a decreasing sequence {Ak}k∈N⊆P(E).\{A_k\} _ {k \in \mathbb N} \subseteq \mathfrak{P}(E).{Ak​}k∈N​⊆P(E). We say that AAA is an E\mathcal{E}E-envelope of {Ak}k∈N\{A_k\} _ {k \in \mathbb N}{Ak​}k∈N​, if there exists a decreasing sequence {Ck}k∈N⊆E∪{E}\{C_k\}_{k \in \mathbb N} \subseteq \mathcal{E} \cup \{E\}{Ck​}k∈N​⊆E∪{E} such that Ak⊆Ck, ∀ k∈N and ⋂k∈NCk⊆A.\begin{aligned} A_k \subseteq C_k, \; \forall \; k \in \mathbb N \quad \text{ and } \quad \bigcap _ {k \in \mathbb N} C_k \subseteq A.\end{aligned}Ak​⊆Ck​,∀k∈N and k∈N⋂​Ck​⊆A.​

Properties of envelopes

The next lemma lists some properties of envelopes which we will be using frequently.

Lemma 5:

  1. If AAA is an envelope of a given decreasing sequence {An}n∈N⊆P(E)\{A_n\} _ {n \in \mathbb N} \subseteq \mathfrak{P}(E){An​}n∈N​⊆P(E), then every subset of EEE that contains AAA is also an envelope of {An}n∈N.\{A_n\} _ {n \in \mathbb N}.{An​}n∈N​.

  2. Two decreasing sequences of subsets of EEE that possess a common subsequence, admit the exact same envelopes.

  3. The collection of envelopes of a given decreasing sequence of subsets of EEE, is closed under countable intersections.

Parts 1. and 2. are trivial, and follow immediately from the definition.

Capacitance

Definition 6: Let EEE be a nonempty set. A collection C\mathcal CC of subsets of EEE is called a capacitance, if

  1. whenever A∈CA \in \mathcal{C}A∈C and A⊆BA \subseteq BA⊆B, then B∈CB \in \mathcal{C}B∈C, and

  2. whenever {An}n∈N\{A_n\} _ {n \in \mathbb N}{An​}n∈N​ is an increasing sequence of subsets of EEE such that ⋃n∈NAn∈C\bigcup_{n \in \mathbb N} A_n \in \mathcal{C}⋃n∈N​An​∈C, there is an integer mmm such that Am∈C.A_m \in \mathcal{C}.Am​∈C.

Intuitively, a capacitance is a collection of “big” sets: the power set P(E)\mathfrak{P}(E)P(E) is a capacitance, and so are the collections of nonempty and of uncountable subsets of E.E.E. The notion of pre-capacity, defined next, gives a more useful example.

Definition 7: A function I ⁣:P(E)→R‾I \colon \mathfrak{P}(E) \to \overline{\mathbb R}I:P(E)→R is called a pre-capacity, if it is

  1. monotone increasing, i.e., I(A)≤I(B)I(A) \le I(B)I(A)≤I(B) holds for every A⊆BA \subseteq BA⊆B, and

  2. ascending, i.e., for every increasing sequence {An}n∈N\{A_n\} _ {n \in \mathbb N}{An​}n∈N​ we have

I(⋃n∈NAn)=sup⁡n∈NI(An).\begin{aligned} I\left(\bigcup_{n \in \mathbb N} A_n\right) = \sup_{n \in \mathbb N} I(A_n).\end{aligned}I(n∈N⋃​An​)=n∈Nsup​I(An​).​

If I ⁣:P(E)→R‾I \colon \mathfrak{P}(E) \to \overline{\mathbb R}I:P(E)→R is a pre-capacity, then for every given real number ttt the collection

C={A∈P(E) : I(A)>t}\begin{aligned} \mathcal{C} = \{A \in \mathfrak{P}(E) \,:\, I(A) > t\}\end{aligned}C={A∈P(E):I(A)>t}​
is a capacitance. Conversely, given a capacitance C\mathcal{C}C, one can associate to it a pre-capacity by defining
I(A)={1if A∈C0if A∉C.\begin{aligned} I(A) = \begin{cases} 1 &\text{if } A \in \mathcal{C} \\ 0 &\text{if } A \notin \mathcal{C}. \end{cases}\end{aligned}I(A)={10​if A∈Cif A∈/C.​​
This then leads to the identification C={A∈P(E) : I(A)>0}.\mathcal{C} = \{A \in \mathfrak{P}(E) \,:\, I(A) > 0\}.C={A∈P(E):I(A)>0}.

Henceforth assume that there is an underlying paved space (E,E)(E, \mathcal{E})(E,E) and a capacitance C\mathcal{C}C of subsets of E.E.E.

Scrapers

Definition 8: A sequence f={fn}n∈N\mathfrak{f} = \{f_n\} _ {n \in \mathbb N}f={fn​}n∈N​ of mappings fn ⁣:(P(E))n→P(E)f_n \colon \left(\mathfrak{P}(E)\right)^n \to \mathfrak{P}(E)fn​:(P(E))n→P(E) is called a Sierpiński’s C\mathcal{C}C-scraper, or simply a C\mathcal{C}C-scraper, if

  1. fn(B1,B2,…,Bn)⊆Bnf_n(B_1, B_2, \ldots, B_n) \subseteq B_nfn​(B1​,B2​,…,Bn​)⊆Bn​ for all n∈Nn \in \mathbb Nn∈N and for all sets B1,…,Bn∈P(E)B_1, \ldots, B_n \in \mathfrak{P}(E)B1​,…,Bn​∈P(E), and

  2. whenever Bn∈CB_n \in \mathcal{C}Bn​∈C, then fn(B1,B2,…,Bn)∈C.f_n(B_1, B_2, \ldots, B_n) \in \mathcal{C}.fn​(B1​,B2​,…,Bn​)∈C.

The first property expresses the intuitive notion that fn(B1,B2,…,Bn)f_n(B_1, B_2, \ldots, B_n)fn​(B1​,B2​,…,Bn​) “scrapes” BnB_nBn​ and the second property ensures that “the scraping does not remove too big a chunk” from Bn.B_n.Bn​. In French, scraper is called rabotage which can be translated also as planing. A simple example of a scraper is the identity scraper: fn(B1,…Bn)=Bnf_n(B_1, \ldots B_n) = B_nfn​(B1​,…Bn​)=Bn​ for all n∈Nn \in \mathbb Nn∈N and for all sets B1,…,Bn∈P(E).B_1, \ldots, B_n \in \mathfrak{P}(E).B1​,…,Bn​∈P(E).

Bn+1⊆fn(B1,B2,…,Bn)andBn∈C.\begin{aligned} B_{n+1} \subseteq f_n(B_1, B_2, \ldots, B_n) \quad \text{and} \quad B_n \in \mathcal{C}.\end{aligned}Bn+1​⊆fn​(B1​,B2​,…,Bn​)andBn​∈C.​
Definition 10: For any B∈P(E)B \in \mathfrak{P}(E)B∈P(E) and C\mathcal{C}C-scraper f={fn}n∈N\mathfrak{f} = \{f_n\} _ {n \in \mathbb N}f={fn​}n∈N​, the sequence {Pn}n∈N⊆C\{P_n\} _ {n \in \mathbb N} \subseteq \mathcal{C}{Pn​}n∈N​⊆C defined by P1:=BP_1 := BP1​:=B and Pn+1:=fn(P1,…,Pn)P_{n+1} := f_n(P_1, \ldots, P_n)Pn+1​:=fn​(P1​,…,Pn​) for all n∈Nn \in \mathbb Nn∈N is f\mathfrak{f}f-scraped. It is called the f\mathfrak{f}f-scraped orbit of BBB.

(Dellacherie, 1972) calls {Pn}n∈N\{P_n\} _ {n \in \mathbb N}{Pn​}n∈N​ above as the f\mathfrak ff-scraped sequence deduced from B.B.B.

Definition 11: A C\mathcal{C}C-scraper f={fn}n∈N\mathfrak{f} = \{f_n\}_{n \in \mathbb N}f={fn​}n∈N​ is called compatible with a given set A∈P(E)A \in \mathfrak{P}(E)A∈P(E), if AAA envelopes every f\mathfrak{f}f-scraped sequence {Bn}n∈N\{B_n\} _ {n \in \mathbb N}{Bn​}n∈N​ with B1⊆A.B_1 \subseteq A.B1​⊆A.

A set A∈P(E)A \in \mathfrak{P}(E)A∈P(E) is smooth for the capacitance C\mathcal{C}C, if there exists a C\mathcal{C}C-scraper compatible with it.

If A∉CA \notin \mathcal CA∈/C, then no subset of AAA can be in C\mathcal CC either by the definition of a capacitance. This implies that there does not exist a f\mathfrak ff-scraped sequence {Bn}n∈N\{B_n\}_{n \in \mathbb N}{Bn​}n∈N​ satisfying B1⊂A.B_1 \subset A.B1​⊂A. Thus AAA is smooth.

If A∈CA \in \mathcal CA∈C and is smooth, then there always exists a sequence {Bn}n∈N\{B_n\}_{n \in \mathbb N}{Bn​}n∈N​ of which AAA is an envelope. Sierpiński’s Theorem

The next result is central in this theory.

Theorem 1 [Sierpiński]: Let (E,E)(E, \mathcal{E})(E,E) be a paved space, and C\mathcal{C}C a capacitance. The collection of subsets of EEE which are smooth for the capacitance, is closed under countable increasing unions and under countable intersections.

We will come back to its proof later. Let's prove some of its useful consequences first.

Theorem 2: Let (E,E)(E ,\mathcal{E})(E,E) be a paved space, and C\mathcal{C}C a capacitance. The elements of the mosaic E^\widehat{\mathcal{E}}E generated by E\mathcal{E}E are smooth.
An easy consequence of Theorem 1, Lemma 2 and the fact that every element of E\mathcal{E}E is smooth because they are compatible with the identity scraper. □\square□

This theorem is very useful in proving some important results. We will discuss two of them. The first one is the metric space version of Choquet's capacitability theorem. The proof of it will be very similar to the general Choquet's capacitability theorem, but we will need Sion's theorem for the general version, which will be the second result.

Definition 12: Let EEE be a compact metric space, endowed with the paving E=K(E)\mathcal{E} = \mathscr{K}(E)E=K(E) of its compact sets. III is called a metric capacity on (E,E)(E, \mathcal{E})(E,E) if it a pre-capacity that "descends on compacts" in the sense that for every decreasing sequence {Kn}n∈N⊆K(E)\{K_n\} _ {n \in \mathbb N} \subseteq \mathscr{K}(E){Kn​}n∈N​⊆K(E) it satisfies
I(⋂n∈NKn)=inf⁡n∈NI(Kn).\begin{aligned} I\left(\bigcap _ {n \in \mathbb N}K_n\right) = \inf _ {n \in \mathbb N} I(K_n).\end{aligned}I(n∈N⋂​Kn​)=n∈Ninf​I(Kn​).​

Fix an arbitrary B∈B(E).B \in \mathcal{B}(E).B∈B(E). If I(B)=−∞I(B) = -\inftyI(B)=−∞ then I(K)=−∞I(K) = -\inftyI(K)=−∞ for any K⊆BK \subseteq BK⊆B, and we have our desired equality trivially. Otherwise, we need to show that whenever I(B)>tI(B) > tI(B)>t holds for some given real number ttt, there exists a compact set K⊆BK \subseteq BK⊆B such that I(K)≥t.I(K) \ge t.I(K)≥t. Recall that

Mixing of Scrapers

Choquet Capacities

Definition 14: A mapping I ⁣:P(E)→R‾I \colon \mathfrak{P}(E) \to \overline{\mathbb R}I:P(E)→R is called a Choquet E\mathcal{E}E-capacity, or simply E\mathcal{E}E-capacity, if it is

  1. monotone increasing, i.e., I(A)≤I(B)I(A) \le I(B)I(A)≤I(B) holds for every A⊆BA \subseteq BA⊆B,

  2. ascending, i.e., for every increasing sequence {An}n∈N⊆P(E)\{A_n\} _ {n \in \mathbb N} \subseteq \mathfrak{P}(E){An​}n∈N​⊆P(E) we have

I(⋃n∈NAn)=sup⁡n∈NI(An),\begin{aligned} I\left(\bigcup _ {n \in \mathbb N} A_n\right) = \sup _ {n \in \mathbb N} I(A_n),\end{aligned}I(n∈N⋃​An​)=n∈Nsup​I(An​),​

  1. descending on pavings, i.e., for every decreasing sequence {En}n∈N⊆E\{E_n\} _ {n \in \mathbb N} \subseteq \mathcal{E}{En​}n∈N​⊆E we have

I(⋂n∈NEn)=inf⁡n∈NI(En).\begin{aligned} I\left(\bigcap _ {n \in \mathbb N} E_n\right) = \inf _ {n \in \mathbb N} I(E_n).\end{aligned}I(n∈N⋂​En​)=n∈Ninf​I(En​).​
Definition 15: A set A∈P(E)A \in \mathfrak{P}(E)A∈P(E) is called III-capacitable if
I(A)=sup⁡K∈EδK⊆AI(K).\begin{aligned} I(A) = \sup_{\substack{K \in \mathcal{E}_\delta \\ K \subseteq A}} I(K).\end{aligned}I(A)=K∈Eδ​K⊆A​sup​I(K).​

Consider a paved space (E,E)(E, \mathcal{E})(E,E), where E\mathcal EE is a compact paving, and define I(A)=0I(A) = 0I(A)=0 if A=∅A = \varnothingA=∅, I(A)=1I(A) = 1I(A)=1 if A≠∅.A \neq \varnothing.A=∅. π(⋃n∈NCn)=⋃n∈Nπ(Cn)∈F.\begin{aligned} \pi\left(\bigcup _ {n \in \mathbb N} C_n\right) = \bigcup _ {n \in \mathbb N} \pi(C_n) \in \mathcal{F}.\end{aligned}π(n∈N⋃​Cn​)=n∈N⋃​π(Cn​)∈F.​
On the other hand, Cn⊆BC_n \subseteq BCn​⊆B for all n∈N{n \in \mathbb N}n∈N and thus π(⋃n∈NCn)⊆B.\pi\left(\bigcup _ {n \in \mathbb N} C_n\right) \subseteq B.π(⋃n∈N​Cn​)⊆B. But (2) implies that the difference of these two sets is a P\mathbb{P}P-null set, and the completeness of the probability space gives the desired conclusion π(B)∈F.\pi(B) \in \mathcal{F}.π(B)∈F.

It is not easy to construct an example of a Borel set in the product space whose projection is not Borel. It requires study of analytic sets. Check out Corollary 8.2.17 in (Cohn, 2013) for more details.

Measurable Graph

The next theorem is a very visual theorem, especially for the case where KKK and Ω\OmegaΩ are R.\mathbb R.R.

Definition 16: For a map f ⁣:X→Yf \colon X \to Yf:X→Y, we define its graph ⟦f⟧\llbracket f \rrbracket[[f]] to be the product set

⟦f⟧:={(y,x)∈Y×X : f(x)=y}.\begin{aligned} \llbracket f \rrbracket := \{(y,x) \in Y \times X \,:\, f(x) = y \}.\end{aligned}[[f]]:={(y,x)∈Y×X:f(x)=y}.​

We call a set G∈B(K)⊗FG \in \mathcal{B}(K) \otimes \mathcal{F}G∈B(K)⊗F a measurable graph, if for every ω∈Ω\omega \in \Omegaω∈Ω its section G(ω)={y∈K : (y,ω)∈G}G(\omega) = \{y \in K\,:\,(y,\omega) \in G\}G(ω)={y∈K:(y,ω)∈G} contains at most one point.

Theorem 8 [Measurable Graph]: A subset GGG of K×ΩK \times \OmegaK×Ω is a measurable graph, if and only if, there exists a set Ξ∈F\Xi \in \mathcal{F}Ξ∈F and a measurable mapping g ⁣:Ξ→Kg \colon \Xi \to Kg:Ξ→K, such that G=⟦g⟧.G = \llbracket g \rrbracket.G=[[g]].

Sufficiency: If Ξ\XiΞ and ggg are as stated, the set G={(y,ω)∈K×Ξ : y=g(ω)}G = \{(y,\omega) \in K \times \Xi\,:\,y = g(\omega)\}G={(y,ω)∈K×Ξ:y=g(ω)} equals the pre-image φ−1(Δ)\varphi^{-1}(\Delta)φ−1(Δ) of the diagonal Δ={(y,y)∈K×K : y∈K}\Delta = \{(y,y) \in K \times K\,:\,y \in K\}Δ={(y,y)∈K×K:y∈K} under the mapping

K×Ξ∋(y,ω)↦φ(y,ω):=(y,g(ω))∈K×K.\begin{aligned} K \times \Xi \ni (y,\omega) \mapsto \varphi(y,\omega) := (y, g(\omega)) \in K \times K.\end{aligned}K×Ξ∋(y,ω)↦φ(y,ω):=(y,g(ω))∈K×K.​
This mapping φ\varphiφ is (B(K)⊗F)(\mathcal{B}(K) \otimes \mathcal{F})(B(K)⊗F)-measurable because of the facts that B(K×K)=B(K)⊗B(K)\mathcal{B}(K \times K) = \mathcal{B}(K) \otimes \mathcal{B}(K)B(K×K)=B(K)⊗B(K), on account of KKK being separable, and that ggg is measurable. Since Δ\DeltaΔ is a closed set (because KKK is Hausdorff), Δ∈B(K×K)\Delta \in \mathcal{B}(K \times K)Δ∈B(K×K) and thus GGG is a measurable graph.

Necessity: Suppose that GGG is a measurable graph, and let Ξ:=π(G).\Xi := \pi(G).Ξ:=π(G). Then Ξ∈F\Xi \in \mathcal{F}Ξ∈F by the Measurable Projection theorem. For every ω∈Ξ\omega \in \Xiω∈Ξ, define g(ω)g(\omega)g(ω) to be the unique element of the set G(ω).G(\omega).G(ω). We want to show g ⁣:Ξ→Kg \colon \Xi \to Kg:Ξ→K is measurable. Indeed for any H∈B(K)H \in \mathcal{B}(K)H∈B(K), it is easy to see that

g−1(H)=π(G∩(H×Ω))∈F,\begin{aligned} g^{-1}(H) = \pi\left(G \cap (H \times \Omega)\right) \in \mathcal{F},\end{aligned}g−1(H)=π(G∩(H×Ω))∈F,​
where the inclusion follows from Measurable Projection theorem.

Debut

Now let K=[0,∞)K = [0, \infty)K=[0,∞), the case important in stochastic processes.

Definition 17: Let A⊆[0,∞)×Ω.A \subseteq [0, \infty) \times \Omega.A⊆[0,∞)×Ω. The debut of AAA is the nonnegative function DA ⁣:Ω→[0,∞]D_A \colon \Omega \to [0, \infty]DA​:Ω→[0,∞] defined as
DA(ω)=inf⁡{t∈[0,∞) : (t,ω)∈A}.\begin{aligned} D_A(\omega) = \inf\{t \in [0, \infty)\,:\,(t, \omega) \in A\}.\end{aligned}DA​(ω)=inf{t∈[0,∞):(t,ω)∈A}.​

Recall the convention inf⁡∅=∞.\inf \varnothing = \infty.inf∅=∞. It is easy to see that {DA<∞}=π(A).\{D_A < \infty\} = \pi(A).{DA​<∞}=π(A).

Theorem 9 [Measurable Debut]: Let (Ω,F,P)(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})(Ω,F,P) be a complete probability space, and consider a measurable set A∈B([0,∞))⊗F.A \in \mathcal{B}([0, \infty)) \otimes \mathcal{F}.A∈B([0,∞))⊗F. Then the debut DAD_ADA​ of this set is a random variable.
For any given real number t>0t > 0t>0, the set DA−1([0,t))={ω∈Ω : DA(ω)<t}D_A^{-1}([0,t)) = \{\omega \in \Omega\,:\,D_A(\omega) < t\}DA−1​([0,t))={ω∈Ω:DA​(ω)<t} is the projection onto Ω\OmegaΩ of the measurable subset A∩([0,t)×Ω)∈B([0,∞))⊗F.A \cap ([0, t) \times \Omega) \in \mathcal{B}([0, \infty)) \otimes \mathcal{F}.A∩([0,t)×Ω)∈B([0,∞))⊗F. To see this, note
ω∈DA−1([0,t)) ⟺ 0≤DA(ω)<t ⟺ ∃ s∈[0,t) such that (s,ω)∈A ⟺ ω∈π(A∩([0,t)×Ω)).\begin{aligned} \omega \in D_A^{-1}([0,t)) \iff 0 \le D_A(\omega) < t \iff \exists \, s \in [0,t) \text{ such that } (s,\omega) \in A \iff \omega \in \pi(A \cap ([0, t) \times \Omega)).\end{aligned}ω∈DA−1​([0,t))⟺0≤DA​(ω)<t⟺∃s∈[0,t) such that (s,ω)∈A⟺ω∈π(A∩([0,t)×Ω)).​

Measurable Section

Let (Ω,F,P)(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})(Ω,F,P) be a complete probability space, and consider a set A⊆[0,∞)×Ω.A \subseteq [0, \infty) \times \Omega.A⊆[0,∞)×Ω. Then for every ω∈π(A),\omega \in \pi(A),ω∈π(A), there exists a t∈[0,∞)t \in [0, \infty)t∈[0,∞) such that (t,ω)∈A.(t, \omega) \in A.(t,ω)∈A. In other words, we can define a mapping Z ⁣:π(A)→[0,∞).Z \colon \pi(A) \to [0, \infty).Z:π(A)→[0,∞). It is convenient to extend ZZZ to the whole of Ω\OmegaΩ by setting Z=∞Z = \inftyZ=∞ on Ω∖π(A).\Omega \setminus \pi(A).Ω∖π(A). When is it possible to choose ZZZ such that it is measurable? The measurable section theorem (also known as measurable selection theorem) says that it is possible to define ZZZ to be measurable if A∈B([0,∞))⊗F.A \in \mathcal{B}([0, \infty)) \otimes \mathcal{F}.A∈B([0,∞))⊗F.

Recall that for Z ⁣:Ω→[0,∞]Z \colon \Omega \to [0, \infty]Z:Ω→[0,∞] its graph is the product set

⟦Z⟧={(t,ω)∈[0,∞)×Ω : Z(ω)=t}.\begin{aligned} \llbracket Z \rrbracket = \{(t,\omega) \in [0, \infty) \times \Omega \,:\, Z(\omega) = t\}.\end{aligned}[[Z]]={(t,ω)∈[0,∞)×Ω:Z(ω)=t}.​

The condition (Z(ω),ω)∈A(Z(\omega), \omega) \in A(Z(ω),ω)∈A whenever Z<∞Z < \inftyZ<∞ can then be expressed by saying ⟦Z⟧⊆A.\llbracket Z \rrbracket \subseteq A.[[Z]]⊆A.

Other than stochastic processes, measurable section theorems have applications in optimal control and game theory.

Epilogue

With this we are done laying the foundations. In the next blog post, we will discuss applications of these results in the general theory of processes.
